title: Pawns on both wings: push, stop or march the king
outcomes: Picks a first move among pushing the free pawn, stopping the pawns on the other wing and marching the king, after checking where the enemy king stands
Sees that one step of the enemy king can change which of the three first moves wins
Recognises a position where none of the three wins

steps.text: With pawns on both wings, start from the pawn nothing opposes: the **free pawn**. Then choose the first move from three: **push** the free pawn, **stop** the pawns on the other wing, or **march** the king. A rule of thumb: push if the enemy king cannot reach your pawn in time; stop if his king is far from his own pawns; otherwise bring your king. Count first.

steps.caption: White to move. The pushes c5 and h6 only draw; the king march Kb4 wins.

line.say: The king goes first. It attacks the pawn on a4, which has no help.
Black's pawn steps forward, still attacked.
White's king steps up the board.
White's king stays close to its c-pawn.
White's king keeps guard of the pawn.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.

steps.text: The rule of thumb needs a count every time. Pushing the free pawn is not a law: it fails when the enemy king can stop the pawn, and then the king or the other wing decides. Stopping is not a law either. In the pairs ahead, one step of Black's king changes which first move wins. Look at where his king stands before you move.

steps.title: Push the free pawn, or bring the king
steps.prompt: In the first position the push a5 keeps the win. Black's king steps one square nearer. Find a winning move again.

steps.title: Push the free pawn, or stop the other wing
steps.prompt: In the first position the push a5 keeps the win. Black's king steps to d7. Find the winning move.
Before each first move: did you look for the free pawn, and then at where the enemy king stands? Which first move did you reach for out of habit?
